title: Multi-Elevator Coordination
description: Design zone-based elevator assignment, load balancing across multiple elevators, VIP/priority floor handling, and emergency mode operation.

segments.text: A single elevator in a forty-story building means unacceptable wait times during peak hours. Real buildings have six to twelve elevators. The coordination problem: when someone presses the up button on floor fifteen, which elevator should respond? Assigning the nearest one seems obvious, but it might leave other floors underserved.

Zone-based assignment divides the building into zones. Elevators A and B serve floors 1-20. Elevators C and D serve floors 21-40. Each zone has dedicated elevators, reducing the average number of stops. One World Trade Center uses four elevator zones with sky lobbies — express to sky lobby, then local elevators within each zone.

Load balancing across elevators considers current load, direction of travel, and distance to the request. The estimated cost function: time to reach the request floor plus impact on existing passengers. Assign the request to the elevator with minimum total cost. This naturally distributes load — empty elevators get more assignments, busy ones fewer.

VIP floors get priority service. The executive floor might have a dedicated elevator that responds immediately and bypasses other stops. Implement with priority queues — VIP requests go to the front. But this creates equity issues. A better approach: reserve one elevator for VIP during peak hours, share during off-peak.

During morning rush, all six elevators are at the lobby going up. Upper floors pressing down get no service for five minutes. How do you prevent elevator starvation during directional traffic patterns?
segments.thought_prompt: How would you ensure down-direction service during morning rush when all elevators are going up?

segments.text: Elevator parking — where idle elevators wait — significantly affects response time. During off-peak, park elevators at distributed floors rather than all at the lobby. If you have six elevators, park them at floors 1, 8, 15, 22, 29, and 36. This minimizes maximum distance to any floor. During peak, park at the lobby for up-traffic and at top floors for down-traffic.

Emergency mode overrides all scheduling. Fire alarm: all elevators return to the lobby immediately, doors open, and elevators shut down for firefighter use. Earthquake: all elevators stop at the nearest floor and open doors. Medical emergency: one designated elevator is reserved for paramedic use with express service. These are regulatory requirements, not optional features.

Multi-elevator coordination requires a central controller that tracks the state of all elevators — position, direction, load, and pending requests. Each elevator reports status updates. The controller runs the assignment algorithm and dispatches assignments. If the controller fails, elevators fall back to independent LOOK scheduling — degraded but functional.

Measure elevator performance: average wait time, maximum wait time, average ride time, energy consumption per trip, and utilization percentage per elevator. Target average wait time under thirty seconds for commercial buildings. Monitor by time of day — morning rush, lunch, evening rush, off-peak — and adjust parking and zone strategies per period.

Design a multi-elevator system for a 60-story hospital. Requirements: emergency preemption, patient transport priority, visitor traffic, and a helipad on the roof with express access. How would you allocate eight elevators?
segments.thought_prompt: Allocate 8 elevators for a 60-story hospital with emergency, patient, visitor, and helipad requirements.

segments.text: Multi-elevator coordination uses zone-based assignment for scalability, cost-function-based load balancing for efficiency, priority queues for VIP service, distributed parking for responsiveness, and emergency mode for safety. The system degrades gracefully from coordinated to independent mode. Design for the failure case first, then optimize for the normal case.
